Title: Learning is Revelation in Disguise: Improved Regret and Equivalence Results for Dynamic Pricing
Text:
Learning is Revelation in Disguise: Improved Regret and
Equivalence Results for Dynamic Pricing
Shiliang Zuo1
1szuo.rs@gmail.com
Abstract
We study dynamic pricing where a seller repeatedly interacts with a strategic, non-myopic buyer who
has a fixed private valuation and discounts future utility. Prior work focused exclusively on posted-price
mechanisms, which only extract binary accept/reject signals. For our first result, we show that menu
mechanisms—offering allocation-payment contracts are able to achive O(Tγ log Tγ) regret, where Tγ is the
buyer’s effective discounted time horizon, improving all prior bounds. Our second contribution is more
conceptual in nature. The problem of dynamic pricing sits at the intersection of two paradigms: adaptive
learning in computer science / machine learning and revelation-principle-based mechanism design in
economics—yet their relationship has remained unclear. We establish a fundamental equivalence: indirect
learning mechanisms and direct revelation mechanisms achieve identical optimal regret. The adaptive,
data-driven algorithms of online learning and explicit type elicitation are two languages towards solving
the same problem; hence, learning is revelation in disguise.
1
Introduction
In this work we study the problem of dynamic pricing: a seller repeatedly offers a product to a buyer over
T rounds. The buyer has a private valuation v for the item that remains fixed across time, while the seller
seeks to maximize cumulative revenue.
This problem was introduced by Amin et al. [2013] and has since been studied extensively Kleinberg and
Leighton [2003], Mohri and Medina [2014], Drutsa [2017], Haghtalab et al. [2022], Drutsa [2020a]. Despite
this rich line of work, two significant gaps remain. First, all prior work focuses exclusively on posted-price
mechanisms, yet there exists a much richer class of mechanisms based on menus—and it is unclear whether
this richer class can yield improved regret.
Second, there is a conceptual gap.
Dynamic pricing lies at
the intersection of two disciplines: machine learning, which treats the problem as strategic online learning,
and economics, which treats the problem as dynamic contracting. Yet the relationship between these two
paradigms remains poorly understood. What is the precise relationship between these two perspectives? We
elaborate on both gaps and present our contributions below.
Menu-based learning mechanisms.
Prior work has focused exclusively on posted-price mechanisms,
where the seller offers a single take-it-or-leave-it price in each round. Yet in principle, the seller can employ
a much richer class of mechanisms: menus. A menu mechanism offers the buyer a set of allocation-payment
contracts, allowing the buyer to select among multiple options rather than making a binary accept/reject
decision.
To illustrate the power of menus, consider first the simpler case of a myopic buyer. In the seminal work
of Kleinberg and Leighton [2003], it is shown that posted-price mechanisms can achieve regret Θ(log log T),
and that such regret is necessary. However, with menus the seller can achieve regret O(1). Specifically, the
seller can design a menu p : [0, 1] 7→R+ specifying a payment for each allocation probability. For example,
setting p(a) = a2/2 yields buyer utility v · a −p(a) in a single round, which is maximized at a = v. Thus,
the buyer’s choice immediately reveals their valuation.
This raises our first research question:

Can menu mechanisms achieve better regret than posted-price mechanisms when facing non-myopic buyers?
We answer this question affirmatively.
We show that menu mechanisms achieve O(Tγ log Tγ) regret,
where Tγ denotes the buyer’s effective time horizon. This improves upon the best known bounds for posted-
price mechanisms: O(log T + Tγ log Tγ) Haghtalab et al. [2022] and O(Tγ log Tγ log log T) Drutsa [2017]—an
additive Θ(log T) or multiplicative Θ(log log T) improvement, respectively. For geometric discounting with
constant factor γ < 1, our regret bound becomes O(1), compared to the Ω(log log T) lower bound for
posted-price mechanisms. Intuitively, menus enable richer information elicitation: the buyer’s choice among
contracts reveals continuous information about their valuation, whereas accepting or rejecting a single price
conveys only a binary signal.
Indirect learning mechanisms vs. direct revelation mechanisms.
Our second contribution is more
conceptual in nature. The dynamic pricing problem has been studied from two seemingly distinct perspec-
tives.
The mechanism design perspective, rooted in the economics literature, views this as a problem of dynamic
contracting Bergemann and V¨alim¨aki [2019], Salani´e [2005], B¨orgers [2015]. By the revelation principle, the
seller can commit upfront to a direct revelation mechanism: the buyer reports a type ˆv, and the seller
commits to a complete sequence of allocations and payments (at(ˆv), pt(ˆv))T
t=1 contingent on this report. The
mechanism must satisfy incentive compatibility (IC)—truthful reporting maximizes the buyer’s utility—
and individual rationality (IR). The seller’s problem then reduces to optimizing revenue subject to these
constraints.
The online learning perspective, prevalent in computer science, treats the seller’s problem as one of
learning through interaction Kleinberg and Leighton [2003], Amin et al. [2013].
The seller posts prices
sequentially, observes the buyer’s accept/reject decisions, and adapts future prices based on this feedback.
This approach appears algorithmic and data-driven, requiring no upfront communication from the buyer;
instead, the buyer simply best-responds to the seller’s pricing strategy.
These two perspectives appear fundamentally different. Mechanism design relies on explicit communica-
tion of types, while the learning approach is adaptive and driven by revealed preferences. The technical tools
also differ substantially: mechanism design employs the revelation principle and solves structured optimiza-
tion problems subject to incentive constraints, whereas online learning focuses on exploration-exploitation
tradeoffs and sequential decision-making under partial feedback.
Yet both frameworks address the same underlying economic problem. This raises a natural question:
What is the relationship between learning-based and revelation-based approaches to mechanism design in
dynamic strategic settings?
We establish that the two approaches are equivalent.
Specifically, we prove that any indirect menu-
based learning mechanism can be converted into a direct revelation mechanism, and conversely, any direct
mechanism can be converted into an indirect menu mechanism via what we call the price equalization
procedure. As a corollary, the optimal regret achievable by learning algorithms equals that achievable by
direct mechanisms.
This equivalence carries several implications. First, it reveals that learning algorithms implicitly solve
mechanism design problems: any low-regret algorithm constructs an incentive-compatible direct mechanism
in disguise. Second, it demonstrates that explicit type reports provide no additional power over preferences
revealed through choices. Third, it offers a unified lens through which learning and mechanism design can
be viewed as two languages for the same optimization problem.
As an application of this equivalence, we provide a simplified proof of the Ω(Tγ) lower bound originally
established by Amin et al. [2013]. By working directly with revelation mechanisms, our proof cleanly isolates
the fundamental tradeoff at the heart of the problem: allocative inefficiency for lower types versus information
rents for higher types.
1.1
Related Work and Discussion
First and foremost, the specific problem we studied in this work is built on the line of work on dynamic
pricing against non-myopic agents. The problem has received significant attention in the computer science
2


community in recent years, categorized under the broader class of problems of learning with strategic agents.
The problem was originally introduced by Amin et al. [2013], with followup works including Haghtalab et al.
[2022], Drutsa [2017], Mohri and Medina [2014]. Extensions to multiple buyers include Liu et al. [2018],
Drutsa [2020b]. The different lens of exploring dynamic pricing against non-myopic agents is explored in
economics literature falling under the domain of dynamic mechanism design (Bergemann and V¨alim¨aki
[2019]). For the case where the principal and agent share the same discount factor, there is a well-known
result: the optimal dynamic mechanism is a static one that pose the optimal Bayesian price, which is known
as false dynamics B¨orgers [2015]. 1
There also exists work that explore the problem from a pure learning perspective where the agent is
myopic and best responds each round. The early work that introduced the problem include Kleinberg and
Leighton [2003] (for which the literature on pricing against non-myopic agents was built upon), and later
also extended to incorporate contextual information Liu et al. [2021], Mao et al. [2018]. Robust versions of
the pricing algorithms were also explored in Krishnamurthy et al. [2021], Zuo [2024].
Our work is also closely related the line of work on contract theory, in particular principal-agent models
with adverse selection (see Salani´e [2005], Bolton and Dewatripont [2004], Laffont and Maskin [1981]). The
textbook by Salani´e [2005] provides an excellent introduction to principal-agent problems; their discussion
on adverse selection problems provide a starting point for some of the results in this work (in particular,
our lower bound result and the design principle of the menu-based indirect learning mechanism). Relatedly,
some work study computational aspects of menus in contract design (e.g. Han et al. [2024], Guruganesh
et al. [2023], Castiglioni et al. [2022]).
Another related work is Albert et al. [2025]; the focus of their work was on characterizing when the false
dynamics scenario can be escaped, i.e., what game structure allows the principal to reason about the agent’s
private type through repeated interactions (when they share the same discount factor). Another related work
is Conitzer and Sandholm [2004]; their work was not on the dynamic setting where “learning” is involved,
and focus more on the computational perspective. They discuss the direct revelation mechanism and what
they call an insincere mechanism, and argue that in the direct revelation mechanism the computational
burden is on the principal, while in the insincere mechanism the computational burden is shifted to the
agent.

2.1
Indirect Menu-based Learning Mechanisms
We begin by describing posted-price mechanisms, the focus of prior work, and then introduce the more
general menu-based mechanisms studied in this paper.
Posted-Price Mechanisms.
In a posted-price mechanism, the principal posts a price each round and the
buyer makes a binary decision to accept or reject. Formally, the mechanism is described by a sequence of
mappings M = (Mt)T
t=1, where
Mt : (pτ, aτ)t−1
τ=1 7→pt,
and aτ ∈{0, 1} denotes the buyer’s accept/reject decision at round τ. The mechanism is announced to the
buyer before the game begins; given M, the buyer strategically responds to maximize his total utility over
the T rounds. Equivalently, such a mechanism can be represented as a binary decision tree of depth T. Each
non-leaf node is associated with a posted price. A rejection moves the buyer to the left child; an acceptance
moves him to the right child. Leaf nodes encode complete interactions of length T. The buyer chooses the
root-to-leaf path that maximizes his utility.
Menu-Based Mechanisms.
A key departure in our work is allowing fractional allocation probabilities
instead of binary allocation decisions. In a menu-based mechanism, at each round the principal posts a menu
of contracts:
{(a, p(a)) : a ∈A ⊂[0, 1]} .
Here a is an allocation probability and p(a) is the associated payment. The agent selects an allocation level
a ∈A and pays p(a), upon which the item is allocated with probability a. The payment is made ex-ante
regardless of the actual allocation outcome ex-post. Formally, a menu-based mechanism is described by
mappings M = (Mt)T
t=1, where

τ=1 7→Mt,
with Mt denoting the menu offered at round t and aτ ∈[0, 1] the allocation probability selected by the buyer
at round τ. Posted-price mechanisms are the special case where each menu contains only two options: (1, pt)
(accept at price pt) and (0, 0) (reject).

Direct Revelation Mechanism
In a direct mechanism, the agent is first asked to report his private type (a “bid”). The report ˆv ∈[0, 1] may
differ from the agent’s true value v. For each report ˆv, the principal commits to a sequence of per-round
contracts
ˆv 7→(pt(ˆv), at(ˆv))T
t=1,
which specify the payment pt(ˆv) and allocation at(ˆv) in each period.
Each pair (pt(ˆv), at(ˆv)) functions as a spot contract: if the buyer continues participating in round t, he
pays pt(ˆv) and receives allocation at(ˆv). The seller and buyer executes this contract sequence sequentially
over time, but the agent always retains the right to drop out at any round. Dropping out terminates the
mechanism immediately. Note that we allow at to take fractional values.
In other words, the interaction in the direct revelation mechanism proceeds as follows.
1. The principal announces the direct mechanism to the agent.
2. The agent makes a report ˆv on his private type.
3. At the beginning of each round t, the agent must decide whether to drop out or not. If he drops out
the game immediately ends; otherwise he receives allocation at(ˆv) and is charged pt(ˆv), then the game
proceeds to the next round.
A direct mechanism must satisfy two key conditions:
• Incentive compatibility (IC): truthful reporting maximizes the agent’s discounted utility among all
possible reports.
• Periodic individual rationality (PIR): at every round, a truthful agent weakly prefers continuing par-
ticipation over dropping out.
Together, IC and PIR ensure that an agent is never worse off by reporting his true type and remaining
in the mechanism throughout. Similar PIR constraints have also appeared in prior work, e.g. Bergemann
and V¨alim¨aki [2010], Balseiro et al. [2018].
To formalize these requirements, we define the discounted utility of a type-v agent who reports ˆv and

Menu-based Indirect Learning Mechanisms: Improved Regret
over Posted-Price Mechanisms
Using posted-price mechanisms, prior work [Haghtalab et al., 2022] achieved regret O(log T + Tγ log Tγ), and
[Drutsa, 2017] achieved regret O(Tγ log Tγ log log T), which to the best of our knowledge, remain state of the
art regret bounds for the dynamic pricing problem. We now demonstrate that the principal can do strictly
better by employing menus of contracts. In particular, we show a regret bound of O(Tγ log Tγ). This is
either an additive Θ(log T) improvement or a multiplicative Θ(log log T) improvement over prior work. If
we consider the instructive case where the discounting sequence is geometric with a constant discount factor
γ < 1, so that Tγ = O(1), then our regret bound is O(1), while previous regret bound is at least Ω(log log T).
Our mechanism operates in phases, maintaining a candidate interval [vt, vt] containing the true type
v. Initially, [v1, v1] = [0, 1]. Each phase posts a menu with quadratic payment function for D consecutive
rounds, then refines the interval based on the agent’s observed choice.

4.1
Converting Indirect Menu Mechanism to Direct Mechanism
The menu-based indirect learning mechanism can be converted to a direct revelation type mechanism by the
revelation principal. For each type v ∈[0, 1], let
H(v) := (at(v), pt(v))t=1:T
be the trajectory generated by the principal’s menu mechanism and the agent’s best response strategy in
the indirect mechanism.
Theorem 2. For any indirect menu-based learning mechanism I, there exists a direct mechanism D with
the same outcome and revenue, i.e, Rev(v, D) = Rev(v, I), ∀v. In particular the trajectory H(v) from the
indirect mechanism is itself an IC and PIR direct mechanism.
The proof is by an application of the revelation principal which we defer to Section B.
4.2
Converting Direct Mechanism to Indirect Menu Mechanism
We now establish the converse direction: any direct mechanism with fractional allocations can be imple-
mented as an indirect menu mechanism.
Theorem 3. Given any direct mechanism D : v 7→(at(v), pt(v))t=1:T that is IC and PIR, the procedure in
Algorithm 2 satisfies the following:
1. After each adjustment step in Algorithm 2, the mechanism is still IC and PIR.
2. The final resulting mechanism I satisfies ∀v, Rev(v, I) ≥Rev(v, D).
The conversion is more involved than the reverse direction (which follows from the revelation principle),
as it requires reconciling type-dependent contracts in the direct mechanism with type-independent menus in
the indirect mechanism.
We represent the indirect learning mechanism as a tree structure, where each node corresponds to a
particular interaction history. Note here that the tree may be infinitely branched, nevertheless it may be
8


instructive to think of the indirect mechanism as having an abstract tree structure.
At each node, we
maintain two key pieces of information:
1. Candidate set: node.values. This is the set of type reports v from the direct mechanism that would
have reached this node (i.e., that made identical allocation choices in all previous rounds).
2. Menu: node.menu. This is the set of allocation-payment pairs (a, p(a)) offered to the agent at this
history.
The tree branches based on the agent’s allocation choice: if the agent selects allocation a from the menu,
they move to the child node corresponding to that choice. The key challenge is price equalization: in the
direct mechanism, different reports v, v′ ∈S may receive the same allocation a but pay different prices
pt(v) ̸= pt(v′). However, in the indirect mechanism, we must post a single menu where each allocation a has
a unique price.
Our solution equalizes prices to the minimum within each allocation probability group. For each allocation
probability a that appears in the candidate set at round t, we set the menu price to pmin(a) = minv∈S(a) pt(v),
where S(a) = {v ∈S : at(v) = a}. We define pmin(0) = 0 for the dropout option. For any report v with
pt(v) > pmin(at(v)), we defer the price difference to the immediate next round t+1, adjusting for discounting
via the factor γt/γt+1. This deferral works regardless of whether the agent receives positive allocation in
round t + 1. The key insight is that IC ensures sufficient continuation utility exists to support this deferral.
After each deferral step, the buyer’s utility remain unchanged, while the seller’s revenue can only go up.
After all adjustments, the menu posted at each node is exactly {(a, pmin(a)) : a ∈A}, where A is the set of
positive allocations chosen by reports in the candidate set S. The full proof appears in Section B.
4.3
Implication: Lower Bound
In Amin et al. [2013], they prove a lower bound of Ω(Tγ) for non-myopic agents. We provide an alternate
proof of this lower bound.
While their argument is framed in the context of indirect mechanisms, our
equivalence result (Theorems 2 and 3) allows us to work directly with direct revelation mechanisms. This
yields a proof that is both simpler and more transparent, and clearly pinpoints how the regret arises from
a fundamental trade-off between allocation inefficiencies for lower-type agents and information rents paid to
higher-type agents.
Consider the case with only two types 0 < v < v. In general, for a truthful direct mechanism, the
following principles hold:
• Lower type: Receives an inefficient allocation (the item is withheld in certain rounds), but the seller
need not pay information rent to the buyer.
• Higher type: Receives efficient allocation (the item is allocated in every round), but the buyer extracts
information rent from the seller.
The above principal generally holds for usual adverse selection problems where the agent’s type is one-
dimensional, and a more detailed discussion can be found in Salani´e [2005]. To understand why, consider
the incentive compatibility constraint: the higher-type agent v must weakly prefer reporting truthfully over
misreporting as type v. In a first-best scenario, the item would always be allocated and the agent always
charged their true valuations. Such is not possible in the second-best scenario when the agent’s type is
unknown. The seller must adopt the following to ensure incentive compatibility:
1. Withhold allocation to the lower type report: By withholding the item from type v in certain rounds
(setting at(v) < 1 for some t), the seller makes this allocation less attractive to the higher type. If the
item is always allocated at the lower type, he cannot be made to pay more than his true valuation,
and hence the higher type should deviate to the lower type and be sure to enjoy the surplus.
2. Leave information rent to the higher type: The seller can give the higher type a utility premium beyond
his participation constraint. If the higher type is left with no information rent, he would of course
again deviate to reporting the lower type. The lower type would not have this issue, since deviating
upward would generally net him no gain.
9


The optimal mechanism balances these two costs. The seller’s problem is to minimize total regret, which
consists of balancing allocative inefficiency, which measure revenue lost from withholding the item from type
v, and information rent: which measures revenue lost from paying rent to type v to prevent misreporting. We
demonstrate that the regret lower bound Ω(Tγ) measures a fundamental tradeoff between the two quantities.
We state the lower bound when there are two possible types. The result of course extends to richer type
spaces (e.g., v ∈[0, 1]), since the mechanism can only have more restrictions.

Conclusion
In this work, we have shown two results. The first is a improved regret via menu-based mechanisms for the
dynamic pricing problem. The second is a fundamental equivalence between learning and mechanism design
for this problem.
We give some comment towards our second result. Our main thesis—that learning is revelation in dis-
guise—reveals that adaptive pricing algorithms and direct revelation mechanisms are not distinct paradigms,
but rather two languages for describing the same optimization problem. We mention two directions for future
research. The first is to characterizing when direct mechanisms can be implemented indirectly. While we
showed that any IC and PIR direct mechanism can be converted to an indirect mechanism in our setting, the
general question remains: what structural properties of a mechanism design problem enable this conversion?
Our proof relies crucially on the ability to defer payments to future rounds while preserving IC constraints.
Understanding precisely which settings admit such conversions—and which do not—would clarify the bound-
ary between learning and mechanism design more broadly. The second would be to extend our results to
multiple buyers and richer type spaces. Our equivalence results focus on a single buyer with one-dimensional
type. Many applications involve multiple strategic buyers with multi-dimensional private information. Does
the learning-mechanism design equivalence extend to these settings? The direct mechanism perspective sug-
gests connections to multi-dimensional and multi-agent mechanism design, but the indirect implementation
becomes significantly more complex.
Beyond dynamic pricing, our results suggest a broader methodological lesson: seemingly distinct ap-
proaches to learning from strategic agents may be fundamentally equivalent. The tools and insights from
classical mechanism design can inform the design of learning algorithms, while algorithmic techniques can
provide new implementations of economic mechanisms.

Abstract: We study dynamic pricing where a seller repeatedly interacts with a strategic, non-myopic buyer who has a fixed private valuation and discounts future utility. Prior work focused exclusively on posted-price mechanisms, which only extract binary accept/reject signals. For our first result, we show that menu mechanisms—offering allocation-payment contracts are able to achive O(Tγ log Tγ) regret, where Tγ is the buyer’s effective discounted time horizon, improving all prior bounds. Our second contribution is more conceptual in nature. The problem of dynamic pricing sits at the intersection of two paradigms: adaptive learning in computer science / machine learning and revelation-principle-based mechanism design in economics—yet their relationship has remained unclear. We establish a fundamental equivalence: indirect learning mechanisms and direct revelation mechanisms achieve identical optimal regret. The adaptive, data-driven algorithms of online learning and explicit type elicitation are two languages towards solving the same problem; hence, learning is revelation in disguise.
